clusters.headline: Nasdaq experiences worst month since March 2025 as tech stocks decline
clusters.briefing: The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.14% on October 30, marking its worst monthly performance since March 2025. The S&P 500 declined 1.29%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.44% to 52,113.50. This broad stock market decline was primarily driven by disappointing earnings reports from technology companies, including Intel and Amazon. Intel's stock plunged 29% on October 31, following a forecast of a sharp contraction in the PC market, increased data-center competition, and rising AI investment costs. AMD shares dropped over 8% in response to Intel's outlook. Concerns about the costs associated with the AI boom, spending, profitability, and cash flow in the technology sector contributed to investor caution. Nvidia and Reddit also experienced declines. Despite several Federal Reserve officials arguing for further monetary tightening, Treasury yields decreased. Oil prices increased, while gold did not benefit from lower yields.

articles.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 30 Oct: It’s a wrap: Nasdaq tumbles as AI costs worry investors; Fed speakers keep hikes in play
articles.description:
• Nasdaq suffers worst month since March 2025 as technology stocks tumble
  • Bitcoin tests key support as Binance security fears weigh
  • Week ahead: Elections, rate decisions and jobs take center stage
  • Earnings next week: Can Apple, Palantir and AMD restore confidence?
  • Fed’s Logan: At least two more quarter-point rate hikes needed
  • Carney: Canada, EU working toward deepest possible partnership, short of accession
  • Fed’s Daly: AI matters for near- and medium-term policy
  • Fitch on UK Budget: Policy continuity leaves a tough delivery challenge
  • Fed's Barkin: Direction of travel is straightforward for the Fed
  • Canada GDP for August 0.0% vs 0.2% estimate
  • US employment cost index for Q3 +0.8% vs +0.8% expected
  • Morning Kickstart: Tech hammered as Amazon and Intel tumble; oil rises despite peace talk
  • investingLive European session wrap: AI spending fears spook tech stocks; dollar falls alongside yields, gold

October ended with investors taking a harder look at the cost of the AI boom. Technology led a broad stock-market decline as disappointing reactions to Amazon and Intel earnings reinforced concerns about spending, profitability and cash flow. Strong demand remains part of the story, but investors are becoming more demanding about when that demand translates into returns.

The cross-market moves were revealing. Treasury yields declined even as several Fed officials argued for further tightening. Oil moved higher, keeping inflation concerns alive, while gold failed to benefit from lower yields. Bonds attracted defensive demand, but the protection did not extend across every traditional haven.

Dollar finishes mixed after recovering earlier losses

The dollar was mixed in the supplied late-session snapshot. Its strongest performance was against the euro, with EURUSD down 0.13% at 1.1164. Its weakest performance was against sterling, with GBPUSD up 0.11% at 1.3390.

USDJPY slipped 0.06% to 157.59, while USDCHF rose 0.05% to 0.8246. USDCAD edged down 0.06% to 1.3979 despite disappointing Canadian growth data. AUDUSD gained 0.07% to 0.7032, while NZDUSD fell 0.07% to 0.5629.

The mixed finish marked a recovery from the dollar’s broader weakness earlier in the session. Falling U.S. yields provided a headwind, but the currency market did not deliver a uniform risk-off response.

Treasury yields fall despite calls for more tightening

Treasury yields were lower across the curve in the supplied snapshot. The 2-year yield fell 6.43 basis points to 4.5917%, the 5-year declined 7.87 basis points to 4.7233%, the 10-year dropped 5.86 basis points to 4.9303%, and the 30-year eased 1.76 basis points to 5.3114%.

The larger declines in shorter and intermediate maturities steepened the curve. The move was consistent with defensive demand as stocks weakened, even though the Fed commentary offered little reassurance that the tightening cycle was finished. Lower yields alone were insufficient to offset the concerns facing technology shares.

U.S. stocks: Nasdaq leads the retreat

The supplied end-of-day index readings showed:

  • Dow industrial average: −573.08 points, or −1.09%, at 51,775.17.

  • S&P 500: −140.32 points, or −1.82%, at 7,580.07.

  • Nasdaq Composite: −747.73 points, or −2.86%, at 25,437.00.

  • Russell 2000: −47.37 points, or −1.66%, at 2,811.84.

  • Nasdaq 100: −1,017.66 points, or −3.46%, at 28,384.85.

The selling extended beyond technology, but the Nasdaq indices carried the heaviest burden. The Dow held up better on a relative basis, although a decline of more than 570 points still reflected a difficult session.

AI faces questions about financing and returns

Amazon and Intel remained central to the earnings concerns. Investors questioned how much spending would be required to sustain AI growth and how quickly that investment would produce stronger profits and cash flow.

A separate Financial Times report covered by InvestingLive added a financing concern: Blackstone reportedly told Anthropic that it might not obtain an investment-grade credit rating after its IPO. This was a reported possibility, rather than a ratings decision, but it sharpened the focus on borrowing costs. Intel was down more than 30% in that afternoon report, with substantial losses across chip and infrastructure suppliers including AMD, Arm, Marvell, Astera Labs and Coherent. Those were intraday readings.

European stocks mostly lower

European markets also finished mostly lower, with the UK holding a modest gain:

  • Germany’s DAX: −221.47 points, or −0.85%, at 25,818.22.

  • France’s CAC 40: −0.58 points, or −0.01%, at 7,969.43.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: +7.73 points, or +0.07%, at 10,729.79.

  • Spain’s IBEX: −204.70 points, or −1.09%, at 18,652.90.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: −501.39 points, or −1.02%, at 49,290.91.

Fed speak: More tightening remains on the table

Today’s Fed commentary carried a predominantly hawkish message, although the speakers differed in how directly they addressed the next policy move. Barkin favored gradual adjustment, Musalem argued for another increase soon, and Logan outlined a minimum of two additional quarter-point hikes. Daly concentrated on AI’s implications for the Fed’s inflation and employment objectives.

Richmond Fed President Barkin described the direction of policy as straightforward, with the pace still open to debate. He favored a gradual approach but pointed to resilient consumer spending, broad business cost pressures and companies preparing to pass those costs to customers. His comments on AI were particularly relevant to the day’s market debate: the investment surge is adding demand and straining supply chains, creating inflation pressures that monetary policy can lean against. His assessment suggested that economic resilience continues to give the Fed room to address persistent inflation.

San Francisco Fed President Daly focused on how AI affects both price stability and employment. She emphasized that those effects matter for policy in the near and medium term. Her remarks did not establish a preference for a hike or a pause. The takeaway was that AI’s effects on the economy are already relevant to current monetary policy decisions.

St. Louis Fed President Musalem delivered a more explicit call for action, saying rates would need to rise again soon. He viewed monetary policy and overall financial conditions as accommodative, with inflation unlikely to ease sufficiently without additional Fed action. Higher bond yields had tightened conditions, but not enough in his assessment. His preference was to act earlier in smaller increments, reducing the risk that delayed action eventually requires a sharper adjustment. A strong economy and labor market supported that approach, while inflation risks remained tilted higher.

Dallas Fed President Logan was the most specific about the amount of tightening she considered necessary. She called for at least two more quarter-point increases to make policy modestly restrictive, followed by a pause to assess whether further action was needed. Skipping a meeting, in her view, would not change the destination. Gradual adjustments could help households, businesses and investors adapt, but she regarded the lack of progress toward the 2% inflation target as unacceptable. Her message made clear that a pause should not automatically be interpreted as the end of tightening.

For traders, the distinction matters: Treasury yields fell on the day, but these remarks did not amount to a dovish shift from the Fed.

Economic data: Labor costs moderate, growth signals soften

The U.S. Employment Cost Index rose 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9%. Wage growth eased to 0.7% from 0.9%, while benefit costs increased 0.9%, down from 1.0%. The report offered some reassurance on compensation pressures, although it did not resolve the broader inflation concerns raised by Fed officials.

Chicago PMI fell to 55.3, below the 56.1 estimate and down from 58.8. Activity remained above the 50 dividing line, but the pace of expansion slowed.

Canada’s August GDP was unchanged versus expectations for 0.2% growth. The advance estimate pointed to a 0.1% decline in September, reinforcing the picture of an economy struggling to build momentum.

German preliminary inflation also came in softer than expected. Annual CPI and harmonized inflation both slowed to 2.8%, below forecasts of 3.0% and 3.1%, respectively.

Oil rises as Middle East risks persist

WTI crude traded at $102.89, up $0.89 or 0.87% in the supplied snapshot.

InvestingLive’s oil coverage highlighted Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and reports of U.S. preparations for potential strikes on Iran. Those developments kept supply risks in focus heading into the weekend. Elevated energy prices also complicated the inflation outlook, even as Treasury yields declined.

Gold and silver join the selling

Spot gold fell approximately $146.24, or 3.64%, to $3,874.33. Silver dropped $3.0644, or 5.88%, to $49.0756. Copper also declined 1.75% to $6.4870.

Gold’s weakness stood out because Treasury yields were lower. That would normally provide support, but sellers retained control. InvestingLive’s gold analysis identified liquidation pressure associated with equity losses as a possible explanation: investors needing cash can sell liquid holdings such as gold to meet obligations elsewhere. That remains an interpretation of the selling, rather than a confirmed explanation for every transaction.

Silver’s larger percentage decline, alongside weaker copper, also left the more industrially sensitive metals under pressure.

Bitcoin remains under pressure

Bitcoin traded at $76,803, down $989 or 1.27% in the supplied snapshot.

The broader retreat from risk assets was compounded by concerns surrounding the reported Binance security breach. InvestingLive’s crypto coverage described exchange-security anxiety and leveraged liquidations as additional sources of pressure. Falling Treasury yields offered little relief as investors weighed both market-wide weakness and crypto-specific uncertainty.

Next week: U.S. elections, jobs and central-bank decisions

The November 2–6 calendar brings several important tests for markets, led by Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections and Friday’s employment report. The results will help shape expectations for government policy, economic growth and the Fed’s next move.

Monday starts with the U.S. ISM manufacturing report at 10:00 AM ET. Wednesday brings ADP employment at 8:15 AM ET and ISM services at 10:00 AM ET. Beyond the headline readings, traders will watch the employment and prices components for evidence of whether activity is slowing while inflation pressures persist.

Tuesday’s midterm elections will determine control of the House and Senate, with implications for taxes, spending, regulation and the administration’s legislative agenda. The September JOLTS report, due at 10:00 AM ET, provides another measure of labor demand ahead of payrolls.

Central banks also remain in focus. The Reserve Bank of Australia announces its decision Tuesday, November 3, Australian time—Monday evening in the U.S.—with several major banks expecting a 25-basis-point hike to 4.85%. The Bank of England follows Thursday with its rate decision and updated economic forecasts. Both events will test how policymakers balance inflation risks against the effects of tighter policy.

Thursday brings U.S. jobless claims and preliminary third-quarter productivity and labor costs at 8:30 AM ET. Friday is the main economic event: U.S. payrolls, unemployment and average hourly earnings at 8:30 AM ET, alongside Canada’s employment report. Preliminary University of Michigan consumer sentiment follows at 10:00 AM ET, with inflation expectations another important barometer. Together, the reports will help determine whether the economy remains resilient enough to support further Fed tightening.

What traders carry forward

The next session begins with three connected questions: can technology shares stabilize, can Middle East risks ease enough to take pressure off oil, and will incoming data justify the additional tightening several Fed officials favor? Friday showed that lower Treasury yields alone are not enough to restore confidence when earnings, financing costs and inflation remain in question.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

clusters.headline: Binance experiences $6.3 billion security breach, largest crypto theft on record
clusters.briefing: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, experienced a security breach on October 30, 2026, resulting in the theft of $6.3 billion in digital assets. This event is described as the largest crypto theft in history. The attack, attributed to North Korean hackers, reportedly unfolded in approximately 20 to 30 minutes. Binance stated that an engineer's laptop was compromised, leading to the breach. Following the incident, Binance temporarily suspended customer withdrawals. The exchange has reported that approximately $3 billion of the stolen funds have been frozen, and Binance intends to cover the remaining losses. Rival crypto exchanges have begun implementing additional alerts and restrictions on fund movements in response to the incident. Some analysis suggests the hackers bypassed standard crypto theft methods. Despite the scale of the hack, some observers note a limited market impact, attributing it to improved crisis management within the crypto sector.

clusters.briefing: US tech stocks experienced a sell-off in late October 2026, with major tech companies shedding nearly $900 billion. This decline was driven by intensifying concerns regarding the high levels of spending on artificial intelligence (AI) and questions about the valuation of AI-related investments. Companies such as Amazon, Intel, Alphabet, Meta, Tesla, and Caterpillar contributed to these doubts through their earnings reports. While Microsoft and SK Hynix were noted exceptions, the broader market reacted to what some described as an AI 'frenzy' that may have led to inflated prices. Reports also indicated that Anthropic could face a junk rating following its IPO, adding to concerns about borrowing in the industry. The tech stock sell-off overshadowed strength in other sectors of Wall Street.

clusters.headline: Bank of Japan reports 2% inflation target met after 13 years
clusters.briefing: On October 30, 2026, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) announced that inflation had reached its 2% target. This achievement comes more than 13 years after the BOJ adopted the goal in an effort to address deflation. Despite meeting the inflation target, the central bank decided to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 1.25%. This marks the first time since 2013 that the BOJ has declared its underlying inflation target of 2% met. Persistent inflation, rising oil and semiconductor prices, and yen weakness have been noted as factors contributing to the inflation trend.

clusters.headline: Reliance Industries Reports Q2 FY27 Profit and Revenue Increases

The company's revenue surged 29% to ₹3.62 lakh crore. RIL also approved plans to raise up to ₹15,000 crore through non-convertible debentures via private placement. Jio Platforms, a subsidiary, posted a 13.7% to 14% rise in Q2 FY27 net profit to ₹8,389 crore, with revenue of ₹40,475 crore, supported by subscriber additions and digital services. In contrast, Reliance Retail Venture Ltd (RRVL) reported a 24.5% fall in Q2 FY27 net profit to ₹2,611 crore, despite a 5.78% to 6.4% increase in gross revenue to ₹91,716 crore.

- Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families — Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families - Fed's Flow of Funds: Household Net Worth Increased $6.1 Trillion in Q3 — The Federal Reserve released the Q3 2025 Flow of Funds report today: Financial Accounts of the United States.
The net worth of households and nonprofits rose to $181.6 trillion during the third quarter of 2025. The value of directly and indirectly held corporate equities increased $5.5 trillion and the value of real estate decreased $0.3 trillion.
...
Household debt increased 4.1 percent at an annual rate in the third quarter of 2025. Consumer credit grew at an annual rate of 2.3 percent, while mortgage debt (excluding charge-offs) grew at an annual rate of 3.2 percent.
Click on graph for larger image.

The first graph shows Households and Nonprofit net worth as a percent of GDP.  

Net worth increased $6.1 trillion in Q3.  As a percent of GDP, net worth increased in Q3 but is still below the peak in 2021.

This includes real estate and financial assets (stocks, bonds, pension reserves, deposits, etc.) net of liabilities (mostly mortgages). Note that this does NOT include public debt obligations.

The second graph shows homeowner percent equity since 1952.

Household percent equity (as measured by the Fed) collapsed when house prices fell sharply in 2007 and 2008.

In Q3 2025, household percent equity (of household real estate) was at 71.6% - down from 72.0% in Q2, 2025

Note: This includes households with no mortgage debt.

The third graph shows household real estate assets and mortgage debt as a percent of GDP.  

Mortgage debt increased by $108 billion in Q3.

Mortgage debt is up $2.99 trillion from the peak during the housing bubble, but, as a percent of GDP is at 43.9% - down from Q2 - and down from a peak of 73.1% of GDP during the housing bust.

The value of real estate, as a percent of GDP, decreased in Q3 and is below the recent peak in Q2 2022, but is well above the median of the last 30 years.

clusters.headline: Comments on December Employment Report
clusters.briefing:
- Comments on December Employment Report — The headline jobs number in the December employment report was slightly below expectations, however October and November were revised down by 76,000. The unemployment rate decreased to 4.4%.

Earlier: December Employment Report: 50 thousand Jobs, 4.4% Unemployment Rate

Prime (25 to 54 Years Old) Participation

Since the overall participation rate is impacted by both cyclical (recession) and demographic (aging population, younger people staying in school) reasons, here is the employment-population ratio for the key working age group: 25 to 54 years old.

The 25 to 54 years old participation rate was unchanged in December at 83.8%% from 83.8% in November.

The 25 to 54 employment population ratio increased to 80.7% from 80.6% the previous month.

Both are down slightly from the recent peaks, but still near the highest level this millennium.

Average Hourly Wages

The graph shows the nominal year-over-year change in "Average Hourly Earnings" for all private employees from the Current Employment Statistics (CES).  

There was a huge increase at the beginning of the pandemic as lower paid employees were let go, and then the pandemic related spike reversed a year later.

Wage growth has trended down after peaking at 5.9% YoY in March 2022 and was at 3.8% YoY in December, up from 3.6% YoY in November. 

Part Time for Economic Reasons

From the BLS report:
"The number of people employed part time for economic reasons, at 5.3 million, changed little in December but is up by 980,000 over the year. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs."
The number of persons working part time for economic reasons decreased in December to 5.34 million from 5.49 million in November.  This is well above the pre-pandemic levels and near the highest levels since mid-2021.

These workers are included in the alternate measure of labor underutilization (U-6) that decreased to 8.4% from 8.7% in November. This is down from the record high in April 2020 of 22.9% and up from the lowest level on record (seasonally adjusted) in December 2022 (6.6%). (This series started in 1994). This measure is well above the 7.0% level in February 2020 (pre-pandemic).

Unemployed over 26 Weeks

This graph shows the number of workers unemployed for 27 weeks or more.

According to the BLS, there are 1.95 million workers who have been unemployed for more than 26 weeks and still want a job, up from 1.91 million in November.

This is down from post-pandemic high of 4.171 million, and up from the recent low of 1.056 million.

This is above pre-pandemic levels.

Summary:

The headline jobs number in the December employment report was slightly below expectations, however October and November were revised down by 76,000.  The unemployment rate decreased to 4.4%.

This was another weak employment report.

articles.title: Comments on December Employment Report
articles.description:
The headline jobs number in the December employment report was slightly below expectations, however October and November were revised down by 76,000. The unemployment rate decreased to 4.4%.

Earlier: December Employment Report: 50 thousand Jobs, 4.4% Unemployment Rate

Prime (25 to 54 Years Old) Participation

Since the overall participation rate is impacted by both cyclical (recession) and demographic (aging population, younger people staying in school) reasons, here is the employment-population ratio for the key working age group: 25 to 54 years old.

The 25 to 54 years old participation rate was unchanged in December at 83.8%% from 83.8% in November.

The 25 to 54 employment population ratio increased to 80.7% from 80.6% the previous month.

Both are down slightly from the recent peaks, but still near the highest level this millennium.

Average Hourly Wages

The graph shows the nominal year-over-year change in "Average Hourly Earnings" for all private employees from the Current Employment Statistics (CES).  

There was a huge increase at the beginning of the pandemic as lower paid employees were let go, and then the pandemic related spike reversed a year later.

Wage growth has trended down after peaking at 5.9% YoY in March 2022 and was at 3.8% YoY in December, up from 3.6% YoY in November. 

Part Time for Economic Reasons

From the BLS report:
"The number of people employed part time for economic reasons, at 5.3 million, changed little in December but is up by 980,000 over the year. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs."
The number of persons working part time for economic reasons decreased in December to 5.34 million from 5.49 million in November.  This is well above the pre-pandemic levels and near the highest levels since mid-2021.

These workers are included in the alternate measure of labor underutilization (U-6) that decreased to 8.4% from 8.7% in November. This is down from the record high in April 2020 of 22.9% and up from the lowest level on record (seasonally adjusted) in December 2022 (6.6%). (This series started in 1994). This measure is well above the 7.0% level in February 2020 (pre-pandemic).

Unemployed over 26 Weeks

This graph shows the number of workers unemployed for 27 weeks or more.

According to the BLS, there are 1.95 million workers who have been unemployed for more than 26 weeks and still want a job, up from 1.91 million in November.

This is down from post-pandemic high of 4.171 million, and up from the recent low of 1.056 million.

This is above pre-pandemic levels.

The headline jobs number in the December employment report was slightly below expectations, however October and November were revised down by 76,000.  The unemployment rate decreased to 4.4%.

This was another weak employment report.

clusters.headline: Wholesale Used Car Prices Increased Slightly in December; Up 0.4% Year-over-year
clusters.briefing:
- Wholesale Used Car Prices Increased Slightly in December; Up 0.4% Year-over-year — From Manheim Consulting today: Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index: December 2025 Trends
The Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index (MUVVI) rose to 205.5, reflecting a 0.4% increase for wholesale used-vehicle prices (adjusted for mix, mileage, and seasonality) compared to December 2024. The December index is up 0.1% month over month.
emphasis added
Click on graph for larger image.

This index from Manheim Consulting is based on all completed sales transactions at Manheim’s U.S. auctions.

The Manheim index suggests used car prices increased in December (seasonally adjusted) and were up 0.4% YoY.
- Light Vehicle Sales Increased to 16.0 Million SAAR in December — The BEA reported that light vehicle sales were at 16.0 million in December on a seasonally adjusted annual basis (SAAR). This was up 1.9% from the sales rate in November, and down 4.9% from December 2024.

Click on graph for larger image.

This graph shows light vehicle sales since 2006 from the BEA (blue) through December.

Vehicle sales were over 17 million SAAR in March and April as consumers rushed to "beat the tariffs".

Then sales were depressed in May and June. 

Sales were boosted in August and September due to the termination of the EV credit at the end of September.

The second graph shows light vehicle sales since the BEA started keeping data in 1967.

Sales in Decvember were slightly above the consensus forecast.

Light vehicle sales were up 2.4% in 2025 compared to 2024.
- Heavy Truck Sales Collapsed in Q4; Down 32.5% Year-over-year in December — This graph shows heavy truck sales since 1967 using data from the BEA. The dashed line is the December 2025 seasonally adjusted annual sales rate (SAAR) of 311 thousand.

Note: "Heavy trucks - trucks more than 14,000 pounds gross vehicle weight."

Click on graph for larger image.

Heavy truck sales were at 311 thousand SAAR in December, down from 336 thousand in November, and down 32.5% from 461 thousand SAAR in December 2024.

Sales were down 15.3% in 2025 compared to annual sales in 2024.

Usually, heavy truck sales decline sharply prior to a recession, and sales have collapsed recently.

clusters.headline: MBA: Mortgage Applications Decreased Over a Two-Week Period
clusters.briefing: From the MBA: MMortgage Applications Decreased Over a Two-Week Period in Latest MBA Weekly Survey Mortgage applications decreased 9.7 percent from two weeks earlier, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) Weekly Mortgage Applications Survey for the week ending January 2, 2026. The results include an adjustment for the holidays. The Market Composite Index, a measure of mortgage loan application volume, decreased 9.7 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis from two weeks earlier. On an unadjusted basis, the Index decreased 28 percent compared with two weeks ago. The holiday adjusted Refinance Index decreased 14 percent from two weeks ago and was 133 percent higher than the same week one year ago. The unadjusted Refinance Index decreased 31 percent from two weeks ago and was 108 percent higher than the same week one year ago. The seasonally adjusted Purchase Index decreased 6 percent from two weeks earlier. The unadjusted Purchase Index decreased 23 percent compared with two weeks ago and was 10 percent higher than the same week one year ago . “Mortgage rates started the New Year with a decline to 6.25 percent, the lowest level since September 2024. Refinance applications were up 7 percent for the week but were at a slower pace than in the weeks leading up to the holidays,” said Joel Kan, MBA’s Vice President and Deputy Chief Economist. “FHA refinance applications saw a 19 percent increase, although that was a partial rebound from a drop the week before. MBA continues to expect mortgage rates to stay around current levels, with spells of refinance opportunities in the weeks when rates move lower.” Added Kan, “Purchase applications were 10 percent higher than the same week a year ago but were down over the week following decreases in conventional and FHA applications. The average loan size was $408,700, the smallest in a year, driven by lower average loan sizes across both conventional and government loan types.” ... The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances ($806,500 or less) decreased to 6.25 percent from 6.32 percent, with points decreasing to 0.57 from 0.59 (including the origination fee) for 80 percent loan-to-value ratio (LTV) loans. emphasis added Click on graph for larger image. The first graph shows the MBA mortgage purchase index. According to the MBA, purchase activity is up 10% year-over-year unadjusted. Red is a four-week average (blue is weekly). Purchase application activity is still depressed, but solidly above the lows of 2023 and above the lowest levels during the housing bust. The second graph shows the refinance index since 1990. The refinance index increased from the bottom as mortgage rates declined, but is down from the recent peak in September as rates moved sideways.
